The blades are among the most expensive components of a wind turbine, accounting for 10-20% of the total manufacturing costs.
Cracks and delaminations are reported to be the most common forms of damage in wind turbine blades, typically occurring close to the blade root.
The proposed SHM system uses SCADA data, which has a low-pass filter applied to it, but is still capable of identifying long-term degradation in blade stiffness and edge frequency.
The training data for the Gaussian Processes is selected from the first two years of turbine operation, assuming the blades were in a healthy state during this period.
The Gaussian Process hyperparameters are learned by maximizing the log marginal likelihood using the Nelder-Mead optimization algorithm.
The case studies showed that the proposed SHM system successfully identified early onset of damage as early as 6 months before it was identified and remedied by the operators.
The computational cost of training the Gaussian Processes scales cubically with the number of training points, which is a limitation of the approach.
The versatility of the proposed SHM methodology means that it can also be applied to offshore wind turbines, where monitoring and maintenance are more challenging.
The use of SCADA data, which has a low-pass filter applied to it, saves considerable processing time compared to higher-resolution data.
The proposed SHM system does not specifically address the challenge of damage localization, as the focus is on detecting the onset of damage using the global response of the blades.
The proposed SHM system takes advantage of the fact that the blades on a turbine are nominally identical and encounter the same environmental and operational variables.
The residuals between the Gaussian Process predictions and actual blade frequencies are used as an informative damage indicator in the X-bar control chart analysis.
The training data for the Gaussian Processes is selected randomly from the first two years of turbine operation to ensure it spans the entire normal operating range of the blades.
The Gaussian Process hyperparameters control the generalization properties of the models and are learned by minimizing the negative log marginal likelihood.
The proposed SHM methodology addresses challenges such as high sensor costs, dealing with nonstationary conditions, and balancing true and false positives in damage detection.
